###

A recurrent theme in the literature is that households face significant upfront capital requirements and uncertainty about the financial returns of rooftop solar, which together deter adoption. Multiple studies list high initial costs, lengthy payback horizons, unclear return-on-investment prospects, and constrained access to borrowing as core financial obstacles to household uptake. (Bagla 2026)

Empirical evidence links affordability concerns not only to absolute cost but also to limited awareness of financing options. In one survey, among households that recognized rooftop solar as expensive yet were not interested in adopting, 73 per cent reported they did not know about available finance pathways. (Bagla 2026) This pattern implies that gaps in financial literacy and knowledge about lending or payment structures can be as decisive for adoption decisions as subsidy levels themselves. (Bagla 2026)

Qualitative work from Karnataka reinforces the role of perceived financial risk alongside procedural frictions: households do not generally reject solar technology outright, but accumulated frictions throughout the adoption journey — including uncertainty about costs and returns — cause many to stall before installation. (Bagla 2026) The Karnataka respondents describe the adoption pathway as procedurally heavy and institutionally slow, which amplifies perceived economic risk and reduces the likelihood that interest converts into purchase. (Bagla 2026)

Policy design therefore shapes financial attractiveness in two contrasting ways. On the one hand, subsidy schemes can materially cut initial outlays (for example, schemes that provide substantial support for larger systems). (Bagla 2026) On the other hand, subsidy-related procedures can add complexity that raises effective transaction costs for households, creating a "subsidy paradox" in which the support mechanism itself becomes an adoption friction. (Bagla 2026)

Cross-state analysis further complicates a simple cost-driven account: inter-state variation shows that some states with modest nominal incentives outperform higher-subsidy states, and statistical tests find a weak—or even negative—relationship between subsidy magnitude and installation counts. (Ranchi 2025) This suggests that the manner in which financial support is delivered, the transparency and simplicity of its access, and complementary measures (for example, financing outreach) are critical to converting incentives into installations. (Ranchi 2025)(Bagla 2026)

Interventions aimed at reducing the financial barrier therefore combine two strands: make the economics clearer to households, and cut procedural transaction costs that magnify perceived risk. Studies recommend targeted financial-literacy tools and standardized "solar finance" materials to present EMI options, payback calculators, and bill-savings estimates; they also propose simplifying subsidy application routes and enabling direct end-user access to reduce vendor-mediated friction. (Bagla 2026)
rows.b:
### Financial constraints

Financial considerations emerge repeatedly as a core barrier to rooftop solar uptake, centered on high initial capital requirements, uncertain returns, and limited access to suitable finance. Bagla (2026) summarises prior studies identifying large upfront costs and long payback horizons as primary deterrents for household adoption. (Bagla 2026)

Household perceptions of affordability often reflect gaps in knowledge about financing instruments as much as raw price sensitivity. Bagla (2026) reports evidence that many households who consider rooftop solar “expensive” are simply unaware of existing financing options; in one survey subset, 73 per cent of households who perceived systems as costly did not know about available finance schemes. (Bagla 2026) This pattern implies that improving financial literacy and signposting of lending products can change perceived affordability without altering hardware prices. (Bagla 2026)

Policy design alters the economics of rooftop installations, but design choices can both help and hinder uptake. Bagla (2026) notes that the PM Surya Ghar subsidy—up to INR 78,000 for systems of 3 kW and above—reduces the upfront burden for eligible systems, yet regulatory requirements such as ALMM and domestic-content rules can raise equipment costs and undercut those benefits for price-sensitive households. (Bagla 2026) At the same time, Bagla (2026) identifies a “subsidy paradox” in which subsidy delivery mechanisms introduce procedural friction that can negate subsidy advantages by increasing delay, complexity, or vendor mediation. (Bagla 2026)

Empirical patterns at state and national levels support the conclusion that nominal subsidy levels are not a sufficient predictor of deployment. A cross-state analysis finds weak or counterintuitive associations between financial incentives and installation rates, including a negative correlation between subsidy percentage and adoption in some regressions, implying that incentive design, delivery quality, and administrative reliability influence outcomes more than headline subsidy amounts. (Ranchi 2025)

Qualitative evidence from Karnataka situates these national patterns at household scale: even where policy frameworks are favourable, perceived financial risk combines with procedural and informational gaps to stall projects before initiation. Bagla (2026) reports that respondents in Karnataka experience perceived financial uncertainty alongside institutional delays and documentation hurdles, and that these compounded frictions help explain the low conversion from awareness to completed installation. (Bagla 2026)

Recommendations emerging from the literature therefore emphasise non-price remedies to financial barriers: targeted financial-literacy tools (for example, standardised calculators and EMI comparisons), deeper partnerships with lenders to widen access, and trialling financing models geared to low-consumption or shared-use households. Bagla (2026) suggests testing a “Solar Finance Kit” and stronger bank/microfinance linkages to increase uptake. (Bagla 2026)

### Financial constraints

Multiple studies identify upfront capital requirements and uncertainty over returns as central financial barriers to household rooftop solar adoption. The literature lists high initial cost, lengthy payback horizons, unclear return-on-investment prospects, and limited access to suited finance as recurrent deterrents cited by potential adopters. (Bagla 2026)

In the CEEW sample reported here, a large majority of households that perceived rooftop solar as expensive were unaware of available financing options; among those who were aware but uninterested, 73 per cent lacked knowledge of such options. (Bagla 2026) This pattern appears in the Karnataka interview data as well: many households stop short of initiation not because they reject the technology but because perceived financial risk and the perceived complexity of arranging payment create a halt in the adoption pathway. (Bagla 2026)

Policy features that on paper improve affordability can nonetheless have ambiguous effects once implementation frictions are included. Central subsidies such as PM Surya Ghar—which provide up to INR 78,000 for systems of 3 kW and above—reduce headline investment needs, but parallel regulatory requirements and procurement rules (for example, domestic content and ALMM conditions) can raise equipment costs and thus blunt the subsidy’s net benefit to price-sensitive households. (Bagla 2026) At the same time, cross-state empirical analysis finds a weak or even negative statistical relationship between nominal subsidy generosity and observed rooftop installation rates, suggesting that subsidy size alone does not reliably predict uptake. (Ranchi 2025)

A related theme is the “subsidy paradox”: the design and delivery of subsidy support may introduce procedural burden that increases rather than reduces friction for households seeking finance. Evidence from Karnataka and national comparisons shows that complex, vendor-mediated subsidy application processes, lengthy approval waits, and opaque steps around net-metering and documentation deter completion even among motivated households. (Bagla 2026)

Several empirical and evaluative studies therefore treat financial constraints as a compound problem of liquidity plus information and procedure. Recommendations drawn from the same evidence base include interventions to boost financial literacy—standardised tools such as EMI calculators and payback estimators—and to expand formal lending linkages with banks and microfinance institutions to widen financing uptake for low-consumption households. (Bagla 2026) These measures aim to shift the barrier set from one of perceived unaffordability to one of manageable financing and clearer subsidy access. (Bagla 2026)
rows.b:
Household decisions about rooftop solar are strongly shaped by upfront affordability, uncertainty about returns, and limited access to suitable finance. Bagla (2026) synthesises multiple studies showing that high initial capital requirements, long perceived payback periods, and doubts about return on investment deter households from moving beyond interest to action. (Bagla 2026) The CEEW survey cited by Bagla finds that a large share of households who consider rooftop systems expensive are nevertheless unaware of financing alternatives, implying that gaps in financial literacy and knowledge of credit options amplify perceived unaffordability rather than cost alone. (Bagla 2026) Karnataka’s qualitative evidence mirrors this pattern: despite policy support, household-level interviews reveal that perceived financial risk interacts with procedural and informational frictions to block installations. (Bagla 2026)

The interaction between subsidy design and household experience also produces unintended effects. Bagla describes a “subsidy paradox” in which the way subsidies are delivered creates additional procedural friction that raises effective adoption costs for households. (Bagla 2026) In Karnataka this plays out when subsidy procedures are vendor-mediated or administratively complex, producing delays and uncertainty that reduce the net attractiveness of subsidies even where nominal support—such as PM Surya Ghar caps—appears large. (Bagla 2026) Respondents specifically reported that institutional slowdowns (for example, DISCOM processing and net-metering approvals) compound financial concerns by stretching payback timelines and increasing perceived transaction costs. (Bagla 2026)

Policy-oriented qualitative work therefore emphasizes that improving access to finance is not only a matter of increasing subsidy size but also of simplifying delivery and raising awareness of financing products. Bagla recommends testing practical instruments such as a standardised “Solar Finance Kit” presenting EMI options, payback calculators, and simple bill-reduction estimates, and strengthening linkages with banks and microfinance to broaden uptake. (Bagla 2026) These measures aim to convert latent interest into concrete applications by reducing informational asymmetries and lowering the cognitive and administrative costs of evaluating and obtaining credit. (Bagla 2026)

Cross-state quantitative evidence supports the conclusion that nominal subsidy generosity is an imperfect predictor of adoption. Ranchi (2025) reports wide inter-state variation in rooftop installations and finds a weak or even negative statistical relationship between subsidy percentage and installation counts, indicating that higher financial incentives do not mechanically translate into higher uptake. (Ranchi 2025) Taken together, the evidence indicates that financial constraints operate through both price and process: affordability perceptions, limited financing awareness, and subsidy-induced procedural friction jointly determine whether households can and will convert interest into rooftop installations. (Bagla 2026)(Ranchi 2025)

Rooftop solar adoption is constrained by a bundle of financial frictions rather than a single cost metric. Multiple studies identify high upfront capital requirements, extended payback horizons, uncertain returns, and limited access to finance as primary deterrents to household uptake. (Bagla 2026) This literature stresses that subsidies and favourable regulations are necessary but insufficient: policy must bridge willingness and installation by easing the household experience of obtaining support. (Bagla 2026)

Affordability concerns frequently reflect gaps in financing awareness as much as sticker price. In one national survey, many households who regarded rooftop systems as expensive had not heard of financing options; this implies that improving financial literacy could change perceived affordability. (Bagla 2026) Policy proposals therefore emphasise practical tools — for example standardised “Solar Finance Kits” that present EMIs, payback calculators, and bill-reduction estimates — to make the economic case clearer for households. (Bagla 2026)

Design and delivery of subsidies affect perceived cost-effectiveness in non-obvious ways. Central schemes can substantially lower nominal upfront outlays for qualifying systems, but regulatory requirements and rising component costs may erode those gains for price-sensitive buyers. (Bagla 2026) Moreover, the administrative design of subsidy programs can introduce its own friction: when subsidy procedures are complex or vendor-mediated, they can increase delays and confusion, producing a “subsidy paradox” in which the support mechanism itself discourages uptake. (Bagla 2026)

Household-level qualitative evidence from Karnataka illustrates how these financial frictions interact with procedural obstacles. The study sampled households that had adopted and those that had not, and it finds that friction accumulates across stages from consideration to installation, so even economically motivated households often drop out before completion. (Bagla 2026) Respondents specifically mention delays from DISCOMs, complex documentation, and uncertainty about net-metering approvals as factors that amplify perceived financial risk and raise the effective cost of adoption. (Bagla 2026)

Cross-state analysis reinforces that higher nominal subsidies do not automatically translate into greater uptake. Comparative work finds substantial inter-state variation and, counterintuitively, a negative correlation between subsidy percentage and installation levels; statistical tests showed no significant difference in installations between high- and low-subsidy states, suggesting that the form, delivery, and perceived reliability of incentives matter more than their headline value. (Ranchi 2025)

Bagla (2026) and related analyses identify upfront capital requirements and uncertain returns as central financial impediments to household rooftop solar adoption. (Bagla 2026) The Karnataka qualitative sample further indicates that perceived financial risk accumulates alongside procedural and informational frictions, so that even potentially cost-effective opportunities do not translate into installations. (Bagla 2026)

Limited awareness of financing instruments is a recurrent theme: many households who judge rooftop systems to be expensive are simply unaware of loan options or subsidy structures, which reduces the effective affordability of systems in practice. (Bagla 2026) Bagla (2026) reports that this gap between perceived cost and knowledge of financing suggests that interventions aimed at financial literacy could change investment calculations. (Bagla 2026) Policy proposals in the Karnataka study therefore emphasise standardised informational tools—EMI breakdowns, payback calculators, and bill-reduction estimates—to strengthen the economic value proposition for households. (Bagla 2026)

Policy design shapes financial attractiveness in multiple, sometimes countervailing, ways. (Bagla 2026) National-level schemes such as PM Surya Ghar reduce nominal upfront burdens through subsidies (up to INR 78,000 for systems of 3 kW and above), yet Bagla (2026) cautions that regulatory choices and domestic-content rules can raise equipment prices and partly offset subsidy benefits for price-sensitive households. (Bagla 2026) The same study highlights a “subsidy paradox”: administrative complexity around subsidy access can create additional friction, meaning that the presence of financial support does not automatically lower effective barriers to adoption. (Bagla 2026)

Comparative evidence underscores that subsidy magnitude alone is an unreliable predictor of uptake. (Ranchi 2025) Inter-state analysis finds states with modest incentives sometimes outperforming higher-subsidy states, and statistical tests show weak or even negative correlations between subsidy levels and installation rates. (Ranchi 2025) These results imply that delivery quality, transparency, and associated non-financial frictions often matter more than headline subsidy amounts. (Ranchi 2025)

In Karnataka specifically, households delay or abandon adoption when financial concerns intersect with procedural delays, vendor-mediated subsidy processes, and uncertainty about approvals; these institutional frictions convert nominal financial support into an uncertain, time-consuming pathway that reduces effective affordability. (Bagla 2026) Addressing the financial constraint therefore requires both improving access to appropriate finance and simplifying subsidy delivery so that monetary incentives translate into timely, trustable reductions in household cost. (Bagla 2026)

The literature frames adoption as constrained by multiple frictions—financial, informational, technical, regulatory and behavioural—so that subsidies create necessary but not sufficient conditions for uptake. (Bagla 2026)

A national survey found that among households who perceived rooftop solar as expensive yet were uninterested, 73 per cent did not know about available financing alternatives, signalling that financial literacy mediates how subsidy generosity translates into perceived affordability. (Bagla 2026) The same review notes that policy design shapes financial attractiveness: for example, PM Surya Ghar provides up to INR 78,000 for systems of 3 kW and above, which can materially lower initial investment needs for eligible systems. (Bagla 2026)

Field evidence from Karnataka corroborates these patterns while highlighting where subsidy delivery falters. In the state sample, adoption stalls because friction accumulates across the adoption stages, so even with a progressive policy framework many households drop out between awareness and installation. (Bagla 2026) Respondents repeatedly reported delays and procedural complexity—such as slow DISCOM/BESCOM processes, cumbersome documentation, and uncertain net-metering timelines—that impede households from converting willingness into completed installations. (Bagla 2026) This accumulation of institutional and procedural frictions shapes the household experience of subsidies: the barrier is not the absence of financial support but the "last mile" interface through which recipients must navigate. (Bagla 2026)

Research suggests testing reforms such as enabling end-users to apply directly for subsidies, simplifying stepwise forms and checklists, and reassessing technical procurement requirements that raise equipment costs for residential systems. (Bagla 2026) Complementary proposals advocate strengthening financial literacy and outreach—standardised finance information kits, lender partnerships, and demonstration sites—to address perceptional and procedural friction that subsidies alone do not resolve. (Bagla 2026)

Cross-state analysis reinforces that higher nominal subsidy rates do not guarantee higher adoption: inter-state comparisons find weak links between installations and conventional economic predictors, and in some analyses a negative correlation between subsidy percentage and uptake. (Ranchi 2025) Together, these findings imply that the effectiveness of subsidy policy depends on delivery quality, transparency, and the surrounding information and institutional ecosystem rather than on headline subsidy levels alone. (Ranchi 2025)(Bagla 2026)

(Bagla 2026) Bagla (2026) reports that respondents experienced delays, complex documentation and unclear net-metering timelines when attempting to claim support, and these institutional frictions discourage continuation toward installation. (Bagla 2026) The Karnataka qualitative evidence therefore connects the existence of subsidy programs to the quality of the institutional interface through which households must apply. (Bagla 2026)

Financial barriers remain salient even where subsidies reduce headline costs; affordability often reflects both capital constraints and lack of awareness about financing alternatives. (Bagla 2026) Bagla (2026) notes that national survey evidence shows many households who perceive rooftop solar as expensive are unaware of financing options, implying that subsidy levels alone will not address uptake unless accompanied by improved financial literacy and clearer information on credit or EMI pathways. (Bagla 2026) The study recommends testing standardised communication tools such as "Solar Finance Kits" to present loan options, payback calculators, and bill-reduction estimates to strengthen the economic value proposition. (Bagla 2026)

At the inter-state level, cross-sectional analysis similarly questions the primacy of subsidy magnitude: one descriptive study found that some low-subsidy states outperform high-subsidy states on installations and reported a negative correlation between subsidy percentage and adoption levels. (Ranchi 2025) That analysis interprets the pattern as indicating that delivery mechanisms, administrative ease and perceived reliability influence outcomes more than nominal subsidy size. (Ranchi 2025)

Bagla (2026) therefore frames policy responses around reducing procedural friction and improving outreach: simplifying application steps, enabling direct end-user subsidy applications (rather than vendor-mediated ones), and creating local demonstration sites to build trust and make subsidy benefits visible. (Bagla 2026) These targeted changes are presented as tests policymakers should run to see whether easing the "last mile" of subsidy delivery increases conversion from interest to installation. (Bagla 2026)

The Kerala study and national survey evidence show that while subsidies reduce the headline cost of systems, households frequently remain deterred by upfront affordability concerns and limited awareness of financing options; many households who say rooftop solar is expensive are unaware of available credit or EMI arrangements. (Bagla 2026)

Empirical work in Karnataka reinforces that subsidies interact with other frictions along the adoption pathway rather than eliminating them. Qualitative interviews in the state reveal that procedural hurdles—document requirements, net‑metering approvals and slow DISCOM responses—accumulate as households move from interest to installation, so that subsidy entitlements often fail to be realised at the household level. (Bagla 2026) These Karnataka findings align with national patterns, where households frequently pause or abandon the process at the institutional interface rather than at the stage of initial interest. (Bagla 2026)

A recurring theme is the “subsidy paradox”: financial support intended to lower cost can introduce additional administrative complexity that increases adoption friction. The literature recommends testing policy changes that let end‑users apply directly for subsidies, simplify application forms into stepwise checklists, and re‑examine equipment rules that raise procurement costs; these measures aim to reduce the non‑monetary burden that currently accompanies subsidy access. (Bagla 2026)

Policy design therefore shapes the economic attractiveness of rooftop systems beyond nominal subsidy amounts. National survey analysis shows that generous financial incentives do not necessarily predict higher deployment; in some inter‑state comparisons, higher subsidy percentages correlate negatively with installations, implying that how incentives are delivered and experienced matters more than their headline value. (Ranchi 2025) Complementary recommendations propose strengthening the household value proposition through standardized finance information — for example, EMI options and payback calculators — and using outreach that reduces perceived complexity so that subsidies are perceived as accessible and useful. (Bagla 2026)

Methodologically, studies combine qualitative household interviews focused on the “last mile” of implementation with broader surveys to link lived experiences to aggregate trends; this mixed evidence base supports the conclusion that subsidy efficacy depends on household‑level pathways from awareness to post‑installation, not solely on subsidy generosity. (Bagla 2026)

Bagla (2026) argues that while policy instruments such as PM Surya Ghar—which provides up to INR 78,000 for systems of 3 kW and above—lower headline capital requirements, those nominal reductions do not eliminate household-level hesitation about rooftop systems. (Bagla 2026) In Karnataka specifically, qualitative evidence indicates that households often reach the later stages of consideration but stall before installation because procedural and informational frictions accumulate during subsidy access. (Bagla 2026)

A key theme in the evidence is the subsidy paradox: programmatic support can create additional administrative complexity that deters users. Bagla (2026) describes how the structure of subsidy delivery—especially when vendors mediate applications—adds opacity and delay, producing a situation where the subsidy itself becomes a source of friction rather than a smooth incentive. (Bagla 2026) Karnataka respondents repeatedly reported delays with DISCOM processes, confusing documentation requirements, and uncertainty about approval timelines; these institutional bottlenecks mirror national friction points and help explain why interested households stop short of completing installations. (Bagla 2026)

Financial barriers continue to matter, but the literature reframes them: affordability is often entangled with low awareness of financing options and weak financial literacy. Bagla (2026) synthesises prior survey evidence showing that many households who perceive rooftop solar as costly are actually unaware of available financing—so that perceived unaffordability reflects informational gaps as much as raw price. (Bagla 2026) In this light, subsidy value alone cannot be assumed sufficient; its effective benefit depends on how easily households can understand, access, and combine it with credit or EMI structures. (Bagla 2026)

Comparative evidence reinforces that subsidy magnitude is not a guaranteed predictor of uptake. An inter-state analysis reported in Ranchi (2025) finds wide variability in rooftop installations that does not track linearly with financial incentives, and even records a negative correlation between subsidy percentage and adoption levels; this suggests that delivery quality, administrative ease, and perceived reliability of incentives matter more than nominal subsidy rates. (Ranchi 2025)

Policy-oriented recommendations in the field literature therefore address both the form and the channel of subsidy delivery. Bagla (2026) proposes testing measures such as enabling direct end-user subsidy applications, simplified checklist-based forms, and revising equipment requirements that raise costs, alongside communication and financial-literacy interventions (for example, a “Solar Finance Kit” and demonstration sites) to align perceived and actual affordability. (Bagla 2026) These prescriptions underline that improving the subsidy experience requires streamlining institutional interfaces and reducing informational and procedural friction as much as adjusting subsidy levels. (Bagla 2026)

Cross-state analysis finds that states with larger nominal incentives do not always record greater rooftop uptake, and in some cases higher subsidy percentages correlate negatively with installation levels; the analysis also concluded no significant difference in installations between high- and low-subsidy states, implying that subsidy magnitude alone is an insufficient predictor of deployment. (Ranchi 2025)

Qualitative evidence from Karnataka aligns with this broader pattern: households commonly encounter procedural and institutional hurdles that negate the intended easing effect of financial support. Respondents report delays and complexities tied to distribution company (DISCOM/BESCOM) processes, documentation requirements, and uncertainty about net-metering approvals; these administrative frictions interrupt the pathway from subsidy availability to completed installation. (Bagla 2026) The study frames this as a “last mile” problem in which the institutional interface for claiming support—not the subsidy quantum itself—frequently determines whether a household converts interest into action. (Bagla 2026)

The research further identifies a subsidy paradox: programme design features meant to help consumers can unintentionally increase adoption friction. For example, vendor-mediated subsidy application procedures create opacity and delays, while technical procurement rules can raise equipment costs and complicate purchasing choices. The study recommends simplifying processes such as by enabling end-users to apply directly, offering checklist-based forms, and revisiting equipment-list requirements to reduce cost pressures. (Bagla 2026) These recommended fixes are positioned as ways to reduce non-price barriers that blunt the effectiveness of nominal subsidies. (Bagla 2026)

Household-level interviews also show that affordability concerns often reflect lack of awareness about financing alternatives as much as absolute expense. In other words, many households who perceive rooftop systems as unaffordable are simply unaware of credit or payment options that would spread costs; one survey found that a large majority of households perceiving systems as expensive had no knowledge of existing financing arrangements. (Bagla 2026) Policy proposals arising from the Karnataka evidence therefore combine procedural simplification with financial-literacy interventions—standardised finance information kits, stronger bank partnerships, and tailored models for low-consumption households—to strengthen the effective value of subsidies by improving households’ capacity to evaluate and access them. (Bagla 2026)

Taken together, the literature reviewed here treats subsidy design and delivery as co-determinants of uptake: the nominal transfer reduces upfront capital needs, but its practical impact depends on clear, low-friction access routes and household awareness of complementary financing mechanisms. (Bagla 2026)

Bagla (2026) argues that supportive policy and subsidy availability are insufficient when procedural, informational and behavioural barriers persist, and highlights the importance of examining how households experience the “last mile” of subsidy delivery. (Bagla 2026) The Karnataka evidence in Bagla (2026) shows this conversion gap explicitly: although many households are aware of rooftop solar, only a small fraction initiate or complete installation, indicating that subsidy presence does not guarantee uptake. (Bagla 2026)

Financial dimensions of the subsidy experience are multifaceted. Studies reviewed by Bagla identify high upfront capital requirements, uncertain payback timelines, and limited financing access as core deterrents to household adoption. (Bagla 2026) The Kerala findings cited by Bagla further show that affordability concerns often dominate other motivations, and that a large share of households who regard rooftop solar as expensive are in fact unaware of financing options—suggesting that lack of financial literacy and awareness can blunt the effectiveness of direct subsidies. (Bagla 2026) Specific subsidy programmes can materially reduce initial costs—for example, PM Surya Ghar offers up to INR 78,000 for 3 kW and larger systems—yet these nominal reductions interact with other cost pressures (such as equipment rules) and household perceptions of risk. (Bagla 2026)

At the implementation level, Bagla documents a “subsidy paradox” in which the subsidy mechanism itself introduces procedural friction that deters households. (Bagla 2026) Karnataka respondents report delays from DISCOMs, complex documentation, and uncertainty about net-metering approvals—frictions that replicate national patterns identified by other surveys and that frequently cause motivated households to abandon the process. (Bagla 2026) The qualitative design of Bagla’s study, focused on the adoption journey stages from awareness through post-installation, attributes stalled conversions to these institutional and procedural bottlenecks rather than to wholesale rejection of the technology. (Bagla 2026)

(Ranchi 2025) To address such gaps, Bagla recommends interventions that reduce perception and procedural friction—targeted communication, demonstration sites, simplified subsidy forms, direct end-user application routes, and practical finance aids such as standardised “Solar Finance Kits” and greater links with financial institutions. (Bagla 2026)
